1.explanation: Prism’s bash grammar (prism-bash.js) defines a comment token that matches any “#” not preceded by a backslash, so it also captures the “#” in URL fragments. The shell-session language (prism-shell-session.js) builds on the bash grammar and inherits this too-broad comment rule. To fix the bug, the comment-matching patterns in both prism-bash.js and prism-shell-session.js (and their minified counterparts) need to be tightened so that “#” inside URLs (or anywhere except at a true comment position) is not treated as the start of a comment.
1.bug_scenario: When highlighting a “Shell session” code block that contains a URL with a fragment identifier (for example: https://…#pre-1-0-9-manifest-spoofing-vulnerability), Prism’s shell‐session (and the underlying bash) grammar mistakes the “#” in the URL for the start of a comment. As a result, everything after the “#” in that URL is colored as a comment, producing incorrect highlighting.

2.explanation:
All of the shell-session grammar lives in prism-shell-session.js (and its minified counterpart). That module is responsible for splitting a shell session into “prompt”, “command” and “output” parts and for invoking the Bash grammar only on lines that begin with a prompt (e.g. “$ ”). Because its current patterns are either too permissive or not properly segregating prompt vs. output, the “#” character is still falling through into Bash’s symbol/comment rules on non-prompt lines. Fixing this requires adjusting prism-shell-session.js (and rebuilding its .min.js) so that:
- Lines beginning with “#” are correctly recognized as a prompt token (if intended as root prompts), or
- All other lines (plain output, including URLs containing “#”) are not fed to the Bash grammar at all, preventing “#” in URLs from being mis-interpreted as comment delimiters or symbols.
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting shell-session code (Prism language “shell-session”), lines beginning with the root prompt “#” or “#” characters appearing in URLs (for example in a documentation link) are not being recognized as prompt or left un-parsed text, but instead end up highlighted as a “shell-symbol” token. In other words, “#” is being picked up by the generic Bash grammar as a symbol (or comment) even on lines that aren’t commands, leading to incorrect coloring of both “#” prompts and “#” fragments inside plain-text output (e.g. inside URLs).
